news.title: Body Language Experts Spot Something In This Wild Clip Of Trump Dictating Tweets To Natalie Harp
news.text:
Footage showing President Donald Trump dictating a Truth Social Post to aide Natalie Harp has recently surged online in the wake of Sen. Jon Ossoff’s comments insinuating that the two spend a lot of time together. 

Interest in Harp has skyrocketed since Ossoff’s campaign rally Sunday, when he said the president “doesn’t want to do the job; he wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie.” Google Trends reports searches for her name have spiked by around 5,000% compared to this time last year. 

The clip that is now circulating is from the second season, fourth episode of “Art of the Surge,” a docuseries on Trump’s reelection campaign that streamed on Fox Nation, Fox’s streaming service, in 2024. The full episode featuring the clip was posted on X (click here to watch) in October 2024 and has since racked up over 9.8 million views. 

The director, Justin Wells, did not respond to HuffPost’s request for comment as of reporting. 

The episode focuses on Trump’s reaction to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ speech at the Democratic National Convention, in which he dictates to Harp what he would like to post on Truth Social. 

“She’s talking about great San Francisco was before she destroyed it,” Trump says at one point while Harp types. “A lot of talk about childhood, we’ve got to get to the border, inflation and crime.” 

Both statements were separate Truth Social posts, shared within minutes of each other on Aug. 22, 2024. (It is not clear why certain words are capitalized in the posts.) 

“[Harp] is laser focused, you can tell with the speed that she’s going on every word that he says — so there’s a really tight connection there,” Traci Brown, a body language expert and behavior analyst, told HuffPost. “At times, his back was turned to her, and she’s still right there on his shoulder. There’s for sure a lot of urgency on her part to please him.” 

While the two are clearly in front of a crew recording the docuseries, Brown said it’s unlikely that the surrounding cameras are influencing their behavior — especially since the cameras cut to other people in the room, including Tulsi Gabbard, Stephen Miller and former Rep. Matt Gaetz, who are not acting the same way. 

“There’s a comfort there between them,” Brown said. “There isn’t any faking it, and if there is, fake only lasts for so long. Obviously they’ve been in [the room] for hours.” 

In terms of whether the cameras had any influence, behavioral scientist Abbie Maroño told HuffPost that, “Trump is focused primarily on the television and reacts quite freely to what he is watching.”

Maroño also noted a clear hierarchical relationship between the two.

“His communication is very direct and matter-of-fact,” she said, emphasizing that he does not seem to be slowly or clearly dictating his statements, as someone might for another person transcribing them. “He does not seem to soften the instruction, explain much, or spend time checking that she understands.”

The pair just seem very comfortable in this situation and environment: Trump knows Harp will follow his instructions and execute them as he wants, without needing to double-check; he also appears very at ease and calm. 

 For Harp, Maroño said she looks “very comfortable” in her situation because ’there is no obvious hesitation or excessive formality in the way she behaves.”

“[It] suggests she is very used to working around him in this way,” Maroño said. 

Is Natalie Harp posting everything on Truth Social?

Harp is not the only person with access to Truth Social, according to reports. CNN White House correspondent Alayna Treene reported in February that Harp “will type out posts that are dictated to her” and Dan Scavino, White House deputy chief of staff, also has access. 

Scavino did not respond to HuffPost’s request for comment. 

“Natalie Harp is one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on President Trump’s team,” Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, told HuffPost. “TRUTH Social is the most powerful and popular social media platform in the world because it serves as President Trump’s authentic voice, where he communicates directly with the American people and the world without the biased media taking him out of context.”

Ingle did not respond to follow-up questions about whether posts are reviewed before publication or who else besides Harp has access to the account.
news.author: Katie Mather

news.title: GOLDSTEIN: Resurrecting Keystone XL pipeline would be win for Canada
news.text:
Keystone XL resurrected by Trump in 2017

The Keystone XL was resurrected by Trump in January 2017 after he defeated Biden, then Biden killed it on his first day in office in January 2021 after defeating Trump. It was partially resurrected by Trump for the second time in April 2026, after defeating Kamala Harris in the November 2024 presidential election.

That said, building the original pipeline today would face numerous regulatory hurdles as well as protests by environmental organizations and citizens’ groups in both the U.S. and Canada, that have opposed the Keystone XL from the start.

The original corporate backer of the project, TC Energy, withdrew in 2021 after Biden vetoed it, costing the Alberta government $1.3 billion it had spent supporting the project.

The current plan is for a smaller version of the Keystone XL, known as the 1,000-km Prairie Connector pipeline, to transport 550,000 barrels of oil from Alberta’s oil sands to Wyoming, partly along the original proposed path of the Keystone XL.

That project is co-sponsored by Calgary-based South Bow Corp. (the pipeline spinoff of TC Energy) and its U.S. partner, Bridger Pipeline.

news.title: Bill Maher reveals Ben Affleck refused ‘Real Time’ return after stormy appearance in 2014 debating Islam
news.text: Bill Maher said Monday that Ben Affleck has rejected yearly invitations to return to HBO’s "Real Time" since the actor branded Maher and Sam Harris’ comments about Islam "gross" and "racist" during a heated 2014 discussion. Maher said on his "Club Random" podcast he had invited the Oscar-winning actor back every year and still hoped nearly 12 years later that a private conversation could resolve their disagreement. "I love him, but we just are going to disagree on that one," Maher said. "I don’t know. Maybe if I talked to him privately, or it’s been, you know, 12 years, maybe I think there’s a middle ground." MAHER SHAMES CLINTONS, KAMALA, DEMS, SAYING THEY WON'T GO ON HIS SHOW OR ANYWHERE THEY AREN'T 'PRE-ADORED' Affleck's representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Maher's account or whether the actor would consider returning to the show. His October 2014 appearance remains his most recent visit to the HBO program. Affleck later explained in a 2017 interview that his response came from his opposition to stereotyping people by race or faith, according to The Guardian. "I love a good debate, and I get very energized by it," Affleck said. "On ‘Real Time,’ I think people could tell I had a genuine emotional response, because I strongly believe that no one should be stereotyped on the basis of their race or religion. It’s one of the most fundamental tenets of liberal thought." SPENCER PRATT SLAMS BEN AFFLECK'S RESURFACED CLAIM THAT 'THE CURE FOR ADDICTION IS SUFFERING' The original "Real Time" discussion included author Sam Harris and New York Times columnist Nicholas Kristof. Affleck rejected what he viewed as sweeping claims about Muslims after Harris said criticism of Islamic doctrine was often mischaracterized as bigotry. "How about more than a billion people who aren’t fanatical, who don’t punch women, who just want to go to school, have some sandwiches, pray five times a day and don’t do any of the things you’re saying of all Muslims?" Affleck said. "It’s stereotyping." Maher defended his criticism during the same exchange by citing threats and violence tied to blasphemy and dissent. "It’s the only religion that acts like the mafia that will f---ing kill you if you say the wrong thing, draw the wrong picture or write the wrong book," Maher said. HASAN PIKER ACCUSES BILL MAHER OF BEING AN 'ISLAMOPHOBE' AND DEMONSTRATING 'ANTI-BLACKNESS' CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Affleck also called the characterization gross and racist. Harris said liberal critics had confused his criticism of religious beliefs with hostility toward Muslims. In a response published days later, Harris said he had distinguished among jihadists, Islamists, conservatives and other Muslims during the discussion. Harris said during a 2022 appearance on "Club Random" that he and Affleck had privately reconciled after the broadcast. Maher said in the new podcast episode he had not had a similar conversation with Affleck. Maher said the enduring attention surrounding the exchange exceeded its significance as an episode of television. news.title: Stephen A. Smith’s problematic commentary still didn’t warrant Black journalists’ harshest rebuke
news.text:
ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith is a blowhard who’s grating, easy to disagree with and dangerously out of his depth when his commentary veers, as it has lately, away from sports and into politics. As he has evolved beyond his role as his network’s best-paid host, he has become harder to ignore, easier to criticize and, many believe, dangerously aligned with a conservative movement that threatens democracy and does real harm to historically marginalized communities, including Black folks, women and immigrants.

If you conclude from the above that I won’t defend Smith after the National Association of Black Journalists gave him its Thumbs Down Award at its weekend convention, you’re half right.

Despite the many valid criticisms of Smith, at this political moment, NABJ slapping him with its strongest official condemnation feels off.

I can only get to half, though, because despite the many valid criticisms of Smith, at this political moment, NABJ slapping him with its strongest official condemnation feels off. I say that not only as a former ESPN senior editor who has seen the results of Smith’s behind-the-scenes advocacy for Black journalists up close, but also as a former three-term NABJ board member. For six years, I was part of the deliberations over who received the organization’s strongest call-out and why.

NABJ handed out a record five Thumbs Down Awards this year, including Smith’s, which was specifically for using his political commentary to disparage Black women. "I was raised by Black women, I have two daughters, I have 10 nieces, I have four older sisters — what the hell are they talking about?" Smith said on NewsNation’s “CUOMO” on Monday night. Attributing NABJ’s rebuke to a “few people” in the group, he said, "I'm a registered independent. I believe in calling balls and strikes and being fair as I possibly can. As a result, you've got people within our community that, if I'm not parroting our speech, then they've got a problem with that, as if we're all one monolithic group.”

In addition to Smith, NABJ called out Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr, Circle City Broadcasting CEO DuJuan McCoy, CBS News and The Washington Post. Among that group, Smith stands alone as, in journalism parlance, talent rather than a media executive. Although Smith is expanding his reach, the other four recipients either are newsrooms as a whole or represent corporate and institutional power that far exceeds Smith’s.

CBS and The Washington Post killed hundreds of journalism jobs over the past year, including jobs held by NABJ members. In 2024, Post owner Jeff Bezos killed the editorial board’s planned endorsement of Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black woman to be a major party’s nominee for president. (The paper’s editor at the time, Will Lewis, said he was philosophically opposed to presidential endorsements.) While he claims otherwise, David Ellison, the Paramount Skydance chairman whose portfolio includes CBS, has nakedly aligned himself with the Trump administration’s crackdown on media independence to win regulatory favor for a spate of media mergers. Those include his intended purchase of CNN and Turner Broadcasting, which could further erode jobs and independence in journalism.

When Ellison installed Bari Weiss to run CBS’ news division, she cut jobs and reportedly inserted herself into editorial decision-making at the flagship news program “60 Minutes,” and CBS fired one of its most prominent journalists, Scott Pelley, after he pushed back against the terminations. (CBS News denies allegations of editorial interference.)

Bezos, Ellison and Weiss operate at higher levels and have much more power than Smith, but NABJ called out Smith by name and only referred to the names of the institutions Bezos, Ellison and Weiss oversee.

Bezos, Ellison and Weiss have much more power than Smith, but NABJ called out Smith by name and only referred to the names of the institutions Bezos, Ellison and Weiss oversee.

The FCC’s Carr is a key figure in President Donald Trump’s effort to use government agencies to put pressure on media organizations Trump deems insufficiently deferential. He’s being sued by the Walt Disney Co. over threats to some of the company’s broadcast licenses and his investigation of Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices. The FCC says the suit is without merit, which is hard to square with Carr’s attacks on ABC late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, his investigation into ABC’s “The View” and the FCC’s early review of ABC’s broadcast station licenses.

McCoy owns Circle City Media, an Indianapolis TV station operator that fired a Black meteorologist, Ashley Brown Elliott, last year. Brown says she was fired in retaliation for challenging what she called the company’s unfair treatment of Black women employees. In the spring of 2025, McCoy issued a statement that said, in part: “Simply put, we don’t discriminate! We proudly have one of the most diverse newsrooms in America which reflects the diverse communities that we serve every day!” Circle City also lambasted NABJ for giving the company a thumbs-down.

"Publicly trying to shame individuals based on supposition should be beneath an organization that claims to advocate for professionalism, fairness, accuracy, and accountability," McCoy wrote on LinkedIn. "The fact that NABJ leadership would permit its name to be attached to such a factless initiative calls into question your judgment, credibility, and commitment to the values you profess to uphold."

Compared with the others in his thumbs-down cohort, Smith’s clout is diminutive, and lumping him in with the rest has dulled what might otherwise be an appropriately loud conversation about who really holds power over the journalism industry and what havoc they can and have wreaked on careers, discourse and public policy. Even though he’s become the most influential commentator in legacy sports media, Smith has nowhere near the power that comes with running a government agency, nor does he have the resources to effect change at the scale of Ellison or Weiss.What he does have is a huge platform on which he’s seen by millions every day, and that was doubtless on the minds of the NABJ board members when they voted to include him. Smith’s lack of institutional power doesn’t make him above reproach, and many would argue that his approach to addressing Black women on his political platforms — it’s notable that NABJ didn’t specifically call out his ESPN show, which he has broadcast live in the past from the group’s convention — gives license to those with their hands on the levers of power to behave in increasingly harmful ways. NABJ has long used Thumbs Down not just as an opportunity to put bad actors on blast, but sometimes to shock them to consciousness and spark a dialogue about how to do better. It wouldn’t be a surprise if that was its aim specifically in Smith’s case.Smith is expanding his own independent media company beyond producing his own Sirius XM and YouTube shows, but unlike McCoy, he doesn’t own broadcast licenses that afford him final say over dozens of journalists or how news gets reported in hundreds of thousands of homes.

If there’s any organization qualified to call out a specific media figure for their commentary about Black women, it’s NABJ.

Despite those important distinctions, Smith should not be considered above reproach. In remarks she gave at the end of the group’s convention, NABJ President Errin Haines, whom I served alongside on the organization’s board, specifically called out Smith for his commentary about Black women. NABJ has long had a tradition of electing women to its top leadership positions, platforming Black women running for higher office and promoting the careers of women vying to ascend both in front of and behind the camera. If there’s any organization qualified to call out a specific media figure for their commentary about Black women, it’s NABJ.

But even compared only with other sports commentators who have conservative political leanings, Smith’s offenses pale in comparison to those of some of his contemporaries. For example, Jason Whitlock, an ESPN alumnus who now makes his living trafficking in the conservative content sphere, has called Serena Williams “classless” and repeatedly made disparaging comments about her body. He has said even worse about his former Fox Sports colleague Joy Taylor, another Black woman journalist.Whitlock has never received a Thumbs Down Award, and Smith, who has a long-running public feud with Whitlock, might be wondering why. Smith, as former ESPN host Jemele Hill noted in an interview with Don Lemon this week, has a long track record of using his platforms to create opportunities for Black journalists, including women. Whether that work is enough to overcome the lurch to the right that seems to be fueling his recent ascent is debatable.But the jury in NABJ’s boardroom has already rendered its verdict.

news.title: Jon Ossoff's Chances of Losing to Republican Mike Collins in Georgia—Poll
news.text: Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff holds a 7-point lead over Republican Representative Mike Collins in the latest poll of the Georgia Senate race, a key race in a state that President Donald Trump won in 2024, which Democrats must defend if they hope to take control of the Senate in the 2026 midterms. The Peach State has become firmly purple in recent years, backing Trump in 2016 and 2024 while backing President Joe Biden in 2020. Ossoff has proven to be a strong Democrat in the state and has been floated as a potential presidential contender as soon as 2028. The new InsiderAdvantage poll released on Tuesday found 50 percent of Georgia voters surveyed said they would back Ossoff in November, while 43 percent said they plan to vote for Collins, a sitting representative from Georgia's 10th District. Seven percent of respondents said they were undecided about how they would vote in the general election. The poll surveyed 800 likely voters from August 16 to August 17 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.46 percentage points. It was first reported by James Magazine, a statewide political publication in Georgia. An Ossoff spokesperson expressed confidence in the senator's chances of winning reelection in November in a statement to Newsweek on Wednesday. “Georgia is a battleground state and Senator Ossoff is already facing millions of dollars of Republican spending against him. The Ossoff campaign will continue to build unstoppable momentum and work to earn every vote across the state of Georgia,” the statement reads. Collins’ Campaign Manager Josh Siegel told Newsweek in a statement that Collins has “cut the gap nearly in half in just six weeks with a fraction of the spending.” “Jon Ossoff can spend all the money in the world trying to reinvent himself, but you can’t buy a new voting record. Georgians are starting to get a good look at the one he has, and they don’t like what they see,” Siegel wrote. The Sabato Crystal Ball rates the race as "Likely Democrat" while both the Cook Political Report and the Fox News Senate Forecast rate the race as "Lean Democrat." Newsweek reached out to the Ossoff and Collins campaigns for comment via email. What Other Polls Show Ossoff, who first entered office in 2021, has built up a lead over Collins in the battleground state, but Republicans still view the race as one of their top flip opportunities in the midterms, along with Michigan, another state that was won by Trump in 2016 and 2024. The latest poll from AARP found Ossoff up 9 points over Collins, 52 percent to 43 percent. It was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research among 1,060 likely voters from July 13 to July 16, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A recent Wick survey showed Ossoff up 4 points with 46.7 percent to Collins’ 42.9 percent. It surveyed 1,175 likely voters from June 27 to June 30, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. A poll for Fox News put Ossoff's support at 56 percent compared to Collins’ 43 percent—a whopping 13-point margin. It was conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research among 1,002 registered voters from June 23 to June 27. Ossoff Leads in Prediction Markets Ossoff’s chances of winning have expanded over the past month in prediction markets. On Wednesday, he had a 91.3 percent chance of winning, up from 87 percent chance one month earlier, on Kalshi. On Polymarket, his chances of beating Collins stood at 94 percent, up from 86 percent one month earlier. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Governor Race Is Competitive, New Poll Finds The new poll from InsiderAdvantage also found that the Georgia governor race between former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, and businessman Rick Jackson, a Republican, remains competitive. Each candidate received 46 percent support in that poll, with 8 percent remaining undecided, according to the poll. Polls have generally shown that the governor race is much tighter than the Senate race. Outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp won two terms and a Democrat has not taken the governor's mansion since 1998. Kemp opted to stay out of the Senate race. The AARP poll found Bottoms with a 2-point lead over Jackson, 48 percent to 46 percent, while the Wick poll showed the race nearly tied, with Republican leading by a half point, 43.2 percent to 42.7 percent. The Fox News poll showed Bottoms leading by 5 points, 52 percent to 47 percent. Jon Ossoff, Donald Trump Dispute Explained The polling comes as Ossoff made headlines this week after taking aim at Trump’s relationship with his aide Natalie Harp. The Senator said the president preferred to “travel with Natalie” rather than do his job as he made remarks about the war in Iran and the record-setting deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier. "While the sailors on the Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings," Ossoff said. "He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn't want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar." Ossoff said during an interview with MS Now’s Jen Psaki on Monday that he has “heard this particular aide referred to as [Trump's] security blanket.” Harp is the president’s executive assistant and was one of three aides who joined him in his recent plane swap, which was prompted by a potential threat of an Iranian missile attack. White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino and Walt Nauta, the director of Oval Office operations, also joined the president. On Monday, Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, reposted a clip of Ossoff's remarks on X, and wrote, "Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics. Instead of denigrating hard working people serving their country, Jon should look deep into his soul and ask himself why he's a miserable person who hates this country. It's because he's a radical, extremist Dumocrat." Jon Ossoff’s 2028 Chances Ossoff is frequently named as a potential candidate in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary, with some in the party believing his popularity in a swing state like Georgia could make him a strong candidate against a Republican candidate nationwide. But the senator has repeatedly dismissed speculation about a potential presidential run. “I have zero interest in running for president in 2028, and frankly zero interest in the 2028 fantasy football right now,” he told Psaki on Monday. But some Democratic voters are still saying they would vote for him in a primary if he changes his mind. Early polls can test name recognition and be an important signal for voters and donors alike about a candidate’s viability. Typically, most candidates wait until after the midterms to announce a White House run and primary season is likely to begin in early 2027. The latest poll from Focaldata and the Financial Times showed 2024 nominee and former Vice President Kamala Harris leading the 2028 Democratic field with 30 percent of the vote, followed by California Governor Gavin Newsom at 14 percent, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 10 percent and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 8 percent. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro followed at 6 percent, while Ossoff and Arizona Senator Mark Kelly each received 5 percent in the poll, which surveyed 2,152 adults August 7 to August 11. Ossoff is also a leading contender in prediction markets, having a 16 percent chance of winning the nomination on Kalshi, only behind Ocasio-Cortez. On Polymarket, he has a 14 percent chance behind Newsom and Ocasio-Cortez. Georgia Is Must-Win for Democrats Democrats likely have to retain their seat in Georgia if they want to flip the Senate. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, so Democrats must defend all their seats and flip four others to take control of the upper chamber. Democrats faced a difficult map, defending seats in two states Trump won in 2024—Georgia and Michigan. Polling in Michigan has shown a tight race between progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican former Representative Mike Rogers after they recently won their primaries. Maine and North Carolina might be Democrats’ top flip opportunities. In Maine, which Harris won by about 7 points, longtime GOP Senator Susan Collins is up for reelection. She faces Democrat Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president. Jackson took over the campaign after scandal-plagued Graham Platner exited the race following a primary victory. Collins has shown a remarkable ability to win elections in Maine as she seeks her sixth term. In North Carolina, which Trump won by about 3 points, former Governor Roy Cooper, a Democrat, has built a polling lead against Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee. Republican Senator Thom Tillis is retiring. The challenge for Democrats is winning those two states and finding two more victories in states that Trump won in 2024. Democrats view Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas as being potentially competitive, and polls show close races in those states.
news.summary: A new poll reveals where Ossoff stands in his reelection bid as he feuds with the White House.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: Jared Moskowitz Is Running For Reelection — Against Hasan Piker And The DSA
news.text:
After winning the Democratic primary to represent Florida’s 25th congressional district, Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.) didn’t thank voters or pivot to his Republican opponent in the November general election. He pivoted to Hasan Piker. 

The prominent socialist influencer had endorsed Oliver Larkin, Moskowitz’s primary opponent. During the campaign, Moskowitz didn’t say much about Larkin or Piker, but as soon as the race was called, he immediately offered sarcastic condolences to Piker on social media. 

“I’ve had to show discipline for the last two months online that I did not know I had,” Moskowitz told HuffPost on Wednesday. “Sometimes you got to let a little air out of the balloon.”

Moskowitz may be the Democrats’ most effective online troll, and he’s got a comedic flair during Capitol Hill committee hearings, but he’s serious about his antipathy toward Piker.

news.title: 5 More Things We've Learned About Trump's 'Human Printer' Aide Natalie Harp
news.text:
More details have emerged about Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old executive assistant to President Donald Trump, who has gained attention in recent days for her undying devotion to the president. According to new reports, the woman who has been nicknamed Trump’s “human printer,” and who was responsible for reposting an image depicting the Obamas as apes, her loyalty goes deep. 

Interest in Harp has swelled with her name jumping 5,000% in Google searches after Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) mentioned her in a campaign speech over the weekend. 

Here are five more things we’ve learned about Harp, Trump’s most dedicated aide. 

She signed a letter to Trump: “With all my heart, Natalie.”

In a letter to Trump reviewed by The New York Times, Harp apologized to the president if she embarrassed him while walking the course with him in Scotland. 

“I want things to always be right between us,” Harp wrote. “I also know I’ve been distracted all week (forgetting to eat throughout the days, and even forgetting to sleep, and only catching a couple hours at a time).”

The letter ends: “With all my heart, Natalie.”

She’s written to presidents before.

According to Harp’s estranged brother, Preston Harp, Trump isn’t her first presidential obsession.

“I’d say since she was, like, 16, she’s had an obsession with, um, gosh, how do I explain this? Um, she’s written letters to other presidents, let me put it that way,” Preston Harp told CNN, referring to George W. Bush.

“And so her dream came true finally,” he added.

Preston Harp told the outlet he hopes his sister wakes up. 

“I love you,” Preston Harp said to Natalie in case she was listening. “I hope that you change and that you wake up and you realize that everybody on this earth is part of a human family and no country is better than any other country.”

She rode in the trunk of a car to be close to Trump.

CNN reported that in October 2023, while Trump was leaving Trump Tower for a New York City courthouse, a “screaming match” ensued after it became clear Natalie Harp wouldn’t have a seat in Trump’s motorcade. With no seat, Harp reportedly jumped in the trunk of a SUV to remain close to Trump.

Melania Trump walked in on her in Trump’s private quarters.

Axios reporter Alex Isenstadt writes in his book, “REVENGE: The Inside Story of Trump’s Return to Power,” that first lady Melania Trump once found Harp in the president’s private quarters at Mar-a-Lago. 

“Harp didn’t do well with boundaries,’ Isenstadt wrote, according to the Daily Mail. “There was the time when a surprised Melania Trump stumbled upon Harp late at night in Trump’s private quarters at Mar-a-Lago, an area that was typically off-limits to those outside Trump’s family.”

“Harp was there to deliver Trump some documents and didn’t want to wait until the morning to give them to him.”

Trump’s other advisers say that with Harp around, the president “enjoys an unvetted flow of information, some of it poisonous and counterproductive,” according to The New York Times. 

There’s footage of her typing out Trump’s social media posts.

In a clip from “Art of the Surge,” the 2024 documentary about Trump’s second win, Harp, who remains mostly quiet, can be seen typing whatever Trump says while watching the 2024 Democratic National Convention and then posting it on his Truth Social account. 

“LYING AGAINST PROJECT 2025, WHICH SHE KNOWS AND SO DO ALL DEMOCRATS, THAT I HAVE ABSOLUTELY NOTHING TO DO WITH!” Harp can be seen typing as Trump says it, referring to Kamala Harris.

news.title: Who is Natalie Harp, Trump's right-hand woman?
news.text:
When a CNN reporter earlier this week asked Trump about Ossoff's comments, the White House reacted angrily later on its official X account, saying the reporter, Kristen Holmes, had taken a "cheap shot" at a staff member.

"Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question," another post directed to Holmes read. "They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive."

Harp's presence as a staffer is nearly constant in Trump's second term.

Reporters at the White House frequently see her standing just feet away from Trump in the Oval Office or boarding Air Force One for many of his domestic and international trips.

"She's always around," one source close to the White House told the BBC. "Literally, always."

Among White House insiders and members of the press, she is often referred to as the "human printer" because she is often spotted carrying a portable printer to provide Trump with hard copies of articles and social media posts, which he prefers.

In practice, this means that Harp has an outsized ability to control what information or updates Trump receives, according to another source familiar with White House operations.

Other anonymous sources have described her to US media outlets as a "gatekeeper" and "comfort blanket".

Harp also serves as something of a social media scribe for Trump, posting to his Truth Social account on his behalf.

In one image that has been widely shared in the aftermath of Ossoff's comments, Harp is shown typing a post - in the president's own writing style - as he dictates to her while watching a speech of Kamala Harris in 2024.

Amid the recent focus on Harp, the White House has described her as a "trusted and valued" member of the team, although Trump has rarely spoken about her on camera.

Ossoff was one of many Trump critics who noted Harp was reportedly on the plane that the president boarded to leave Turkey after the US supposedly received information about a threat from Iran.

Reporter Haberman, who has also reported extensively on Trump's presidencies, was asked during an appearance on the news network MSNOW why Trump took Harp with him on the secret plane: "Because she is sort of his binky, for lack of a better way of putting it, a comfort blanket."

Haberman and Swan reported for the New York Times in 2024 that Harp had supposedly written in a letter to Trump: "You are all that matters to me."

news.title: The Left Has a Working-Class Problem
news.text:
In a recent column published by the New Republic, Michael Tomasky asks, “Why don’t lefty candidates do better among working-class voters?” This shouldn’t be a mystery considering that Donald Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris in 2024 was delivered by a multiracial working-class coalition. He accomplished that historic feat by building his campaign platform around the things working-class voters care about. The real mystery is why anyone is still struggling to understand this obvious fact. Tomasky does at least grasp that, even in the recent Democratic primary in Michigan, far left candidate Abdul El-Sayed underperformed so badly among working class voters that it very nearly cost him the nomination.

Part of the problem is that our friends on the left don’t understand how to define “working class.” Being intellectually lazy, they rely on the standard academic definition of the working class — adult workers lacking a four-year college degree. “By that measure,” writes José García of the Ford Foundation, “the working class constitutes over 60 percent of the U.S. labor force — more than 93 million people as of 2023. This group is not only large, but richly diverse: Roughly 53 percent are non-Hispanic white, 13 percent black, and 25 percent Hispanic.” Yet this academic definition of working class has little or no meaning to its actual members. Political scientist Nicholas Jacobs explains in The Conversation that the fabled “diploma divide” isn’t a satisfactory definition:

While a larger proportion of the electorate has obtained a college degree and household incomes have risen, the share of Americans who consider themselves working class has remained remarkably stable: roughly 35 percent of voters for the past 70 years, 38 percent in 2024.… There are conventional ways to define the working class, but they often miss how people understand their own place in society. In the 2024 American National Election Studies, for example, 21 percent of those who identify as working class have a college degree, only 5 percent belong to a private-sector union, and 37 percent own stocks. Conversely, most Americans without a college degree do not identify as working class.

Despite its limitations, the diploma divide is routinely cited by the commentariat as the most reliable predictor of voting behavior in modern democracies. College-educated voters increasingly support the Democratic Party, while non-college voters lean heavily toward the Republican. news.title: Data center backlash poised to play critical role in midterms: ‘We don’t even need data centers’
news.text:
Big Tech has failed to win over Americans on its rapid build-out of data centers – and souring public opinion on the power-hungry sites could play a critical role in midterm elections across the country.

People would rather see a nuclear power plant built in their neighborhood than a data center, a May Gallup poll found, with a whopping 71% of Americans opposed to the latter. 

In comparison, 53% opposed new nuclear energy plants.

This new form of NIMBYism is taking hold on both ends of the political spectrum, and the share of voters who oppose data center construction is growing, according to a July survey conducted by independent polling group Public First. 

In January, people who said they voted for Democratic Kamala Harris for president in 2024 were split on the issue, with 36% saying they would support a data center being built within three miles of their home and 33% saying they would not. 

By July, 53% of Harris voters opposed a data center site, while just 22% said they would support it.

Even among those who voted for Republican President Trump — who has praised the rapid rise of AI for drawing billions of dollars in infrastructure investment and potentially creating swaths of jobs — 33% said they would oppose a data center, up from 26% in July. 

The share who said they would support a data center project dropped nine percentage points to 34%.

Increasingly negative opinions of the emerging tech could play a pivotal role in elections around the nation, as more than 200 data centers are being built in dozens of competitive House districts, according to a recent Politico analysis.

Politicians on both sides of the aisle are eager to separate themselves from the controversial centers as their seats are up for grabs this fall – but many are unsure just how far to go in their efforts to limit new construction.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a potential Democratic presidential contender in 2028, recently signed an executive order restricting data center development in the state, taking a stand against what he called “predatory” developers.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, issued a pause on data center approvals and created a set of standards that several companies agreed to follow regarding water and electricity use and quality-of-life for nearby residents. 

He said another company that refused to comply with his requirements has dropped its project.

In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul in July issued a first-of-its-kind moratorium on large-scale data center construction – though it has drawn backlash from AI supporters who warn the ban could quash construction jobs. Other critics fear the regulation isn’t strict enough.

Tech firms like Google, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft – four of the largest data center builders – are anxiously trying to turn the tide as they seek looser government regulations on the rollout of new AI products.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg launched an AI optimism campaign this summer, writing in a Wall Street Journal op-ed that the new tech will unlock widespread prosperity. He even argued against potential US bans on AI models from US rival China.

OpenAI has released a flurry of ads that paint its technology in a positive light, including one that shows a young man using ChatGPT to find a recipe to impress his date and another that shows an elderly woman knitting as she chit-chats with the AI bot.

But the messaging appears to be getting drowned out by horror stories that consistently turn up in online searches about data centers.

Social media users who oppose data centers have cited environmental issues, noise and light pollution and economic concerns, like the potential for the new tech to eradicate many jobs.

One TikTok video with over 11 million views shows a homeowner in Dowagiac, Mich., sitting on a porch and listening to a high-pitched whining sound that allegedly comes from a nearby data center 24/7.

Last month, residents there launched a class action lawsuit against Hyperscale Data, the site operator, over allegations of excessive noise pollution. 

Hyperscale has said it remains “committed to being a good neighbor” and is working to reduce sound levels in the area.

One woman, Ansley Brown, racked up millions of views on Instagram and TikTok with videos alleging that Georgia Power was seizing her childhood home to tear it down and expand existing power lines to support data center projects, including a large site in Fayetteville.

Georgia Power has denied the allegations. Brown said her congressman, Republican Rep. Brian Jack, helped connect her with Georgia Power. According to reports, her family has settled with the utility for an undisclosed amount.

In another social media video, a young woman says that the Pennsylvania golf course where she has been working each summer is being closed and turned into a data center.

Such videos have been flooded with comments calling for tighter regulations of data center build-outs, with some demanding total bans.

“We don’t even need data centers,” said one commenter, who racked up more than 75,000 likes.
news.summary: Big Tech has failed to win over Americans on its rapid build-out of data centers – and souring public opinion could play a critical role in midterm elections.

news.title: Will Caribbean Born Candidates Prevail In Today’s Florida Primary?  - Dominican Republic Post – Caribbean
news.text:
News Americas, Fort Lauderdale, FL, Tues. Aug. 18, 2026: Several Caribbean-born candidates are hoping to make history in the Florida Primary election today as voting got underway early this morning.

Two Haitian-born immigrants are among a crowded field of candidates seeking to succeed retiring U.S. Rep. Frederica Wilson in Florida’s 24th Congressional District, setting up a race that could make history for one of the nation’s largest Haitian-American communities.

Former Miami-Dade County Commissioner Jean Monestime and physician Dr. Rudolph Moise are both seeking the Democratic nomination, hoping to become the first Haitians elected to represent the district in Congress. Wilson, who has represented the heavily Democratic Miami Gardens-based district since 2011, announced earlier this year that she would not seek another term, triggering a crowded primary.

Monestime, born in Haiti, arrived in the United States alone at age 17 without speaking English. He later earned finance and business degrees from Florida International University and Nova Southeastern University before becoming the first Haitian American elected to the Miami-Dade County Commission, and later its first Haitian-born chairman, championing infrastructure improvements and neighborhood revitalization across North Miami-Dade during his 12 years on the commission.

Moise, a physician, attorney, and entrepreneur born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, is making his third bid for the seat after previously challenging Wilson. After immigrating to the U.S. as a teenager, he served in the U.S. Air Force before earning degrees from the University of Illinois Chicago and the Chicago College of Osteopathic Medicine. In Miami, he built a medical practice serving many Haitian refugees and later founded the city’s first full-time Creole-language radio station, Radio Carnivale.

The Democratic primary field also includes former State Senator Shevrin Jones, Miami-Dade Commissioner Oliver Gilbert III, who has Wilson’s endorsement, Kendrick Meek Jr., attorney Roderick Vereen, and Marshall Davis Sr., longtime director of the African Heritage Cultural Arts Center in Liberty City. Republicans Te Mayonna Brown and Andy Daro are also on the ballot.

Elsewhere on Tuesday’s ballot, Jamaica-born Dale Holness is making his third attempt to win Florida’s Congressional District 20, having lost a 2020 special election by just five votes. A win would make him the first Jamaica-born member of the U.S. Congress. He faces a crowded field, including redistricted incumbent Debbie Wasserman Schultz, Haitian American former Congresswoman Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, who represented the district from 2022 until her resignation in April 2026 under a federal indictment; Luther Campbell and Elijah Manley. Holness said he’s raised more than $200,000 toward a $1 million goal, building his campaign around affordability, citing that 13% of Floridians currently live in poverty.

Kaysia Earley, who has Jamaican roots, is running in Congressional District 22, campaigning on what she calls “Faith. Family. Future.” A trial attorney and founder of Seeds of Manna, Earley is a first-time congressional candidate after a previous unsuccessful run for a judgeship.

On the Republican side, Jamaican Carla Spaulding is competing in a four-way primary for District 20.

Elsewhere on the ballot, Jamaicans Tamar Hamilton and Veronica Walker are also both running for judgeships.

In the Republican Primary Byron Donalds, the Jamaican-roots current U.S. Representative, serves on the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability and House Financial Services Committee is in the race to replace Gov. Ron DeSantis who is term-limited as is Cuban American attorney Rachel Rodriguez who has worked for the Vires Law Group PLLC in West Palm Beach since 2022 and also founded Paragon Law Group, PLLC in March 2025.

While in the Democratic Primary the seat, Dotie Joseph a Haitian-born attorney and term-limited state representative from North Miami, is among the candidates on the ticket.

In Coral Springs, Florida, Marly Metayer, a longtime registered nurse and Haitian immigrant, is running for the City Commission seat left vacant after the tragic death of her daughter, Vice Mayor Nancy Metayer Bowen, earlier this year. City leaders opted to let voters choose a successor rather than appoint one to finish Metayer Bowen’s term. Metayer Bowen was allegedly murdered by her Jamaican-born husband in April.

If elected, Metayer would follow directly in her daughter’s footsteps. Metayer Bowen made history in 2020 as the first Black and Haitian American woman elected to the Coral Springs City Commission, winning re-election unopposed in 2024 and becoming vice mayor in 2025. She also served as Florida’s Caribbean Vote Director for Kamala Harris’ 2024 presidential campaign before she was fatally shot in April in what authorities described as a domestic violence incident. Her husband, Stephen Bowen, has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder and remains in custody awaiting trial.

“She really felt like she wanted to continue the work that Nancy was doing,” said campaign manager David Metellus, who also managed Metayer Bowen’s campaigns. “She taught her kids to never leave a job undone.”

Born in Haiti, Marly Metayer immigrated to the U.S. at age 13, graduated from Dillard High School, and has worked as a registered nurse for more than 35 years. A Coral Springs resident since 1999, she hopes to build on her daughter’s focus on environmental justice, public safety and economic opportunity, with added emphasis on mental and behavioral health, following what her family has called an extraordinarily difficult year: she lost her youngest son, Donovan, to suicide in late 2025, just months before Nancy’s death. Other qualified candidates for the seat include William “Bill” Capplis, Adeline Darius, Erick Nyatenya and Terry Williams Edden.

Florida Secretary of State Cord Byrd is urging residents to participate, reminding voters that polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time on Tuesday. “I encourage all Florida voters to exercise their right to vote,” Byrd said.

Voters must present a current, valid photo ID to vote, and those in line by 7 p.m. will still be permitted to cast a ballot. Preliminary unofficial results will begin posting on the Florida Election Watch website after 8 p.m. Eastern time.

NewsAmericasNow will continue tracking Caribbean candidates across Florida’s primary and general elections.

news.title: Kamala Harris's friend sues British Airways after 'she was accidentally hit by cabin crew dealing with a disruptive passenger'
news.text:
Kamala Harris' friend is suing British Airways after claiming she was caught in a row onboard that resulted in her being hit in the head by a crew member.

Karen Gibbs, a former US navy lawyer, said she got caught in the crossfire after a member of staff was dealing with a disruptive passenger and received a 'forceful blow'.

Ms Gibbs said she was left with 'head pain, blurred vision, dizziness, disorientation and distress', according to The Times.

Medical professionals have advised that her symptoms were consistent with a migraine. 

The former Vice President's university friend has claimed the major airline only provided an ice pack to help soothe the injury and offered medical attention on board 90 minutes after the incident.

She alleged that after she wrote a complaint to British Airways she was offered a £50 payment in good faith.

The lawsuit alleges that upon landing Ms Gibbs was unable to walk through the airport without the assistance of a wheelchair. 

Documents claim Ms Gibbs experienced 'continuing migraines or headaches, vision disturbance, memory and concentration problems, cognitive fatigue, disorientation, balance problem and other post-concussive symptoms'.

The incident occurred in August 2024 when she was travelling from Heathrow to Washington.

The cabin crew involved had intervened with a passenger who was causing issues on the flight, while Ms Gibbs was an 'innocent bystander' that accidentally got hit on top of her head.

Ms Gibbs has claimed the accident left her with a lasting physical toll on her body which forced her to retire from her new job as a senior federal attorney in the US civil service early due to suffering 'cognitive fatigue', concentration problems and memory problems.

The claim said: 'Before the incident, Plaintiff [Gibbs] was active, independent, mentally sharp and capable of performing demanding legal work and extensive family, church, civic and travel responsibilities. 

'Family members, friends and medical professionals observed a marked decline after the incident.'

Ms Gibbs is seeking damages for past and future medical expenses, lost compensation and employment benefits, mental anguish and 'loss of enjoyment of life'.

British Airways said: 'As this matter is the subject of ongoing legal proceedings, it would be inappropriate for us to comment.'

The federal lawyer spent 26 years working for the US navy and went on to serve as senior counsel at the Department of Justice organised crime drug enforcement task force.

Ms Gibbs went to the former Democratic Vice President's inauguration and was godmother to her children. They met at Howard University in Washington in the 1980s.

news.title: The Gen Z Whisperer on How Democrats Can Win the Midterms
news.text:
Adam Mockler is the Energizer Bunny of liberal debate bros. When he’s not getting into it with CNN personality Scott Jennings, the 23-year-old hosts the podcast The Adam Mockler Show and runs a popular YouTube channel. And following Donald Trump’s success with young men in 2024, he has carved out a niche for himself as a Gen Z whisperer.

Mockler’s kind of a funny guy. If you squint and look at him one way, he seems like a moderate, but look at him from another angle, and he seems super progressive. In a way, he’s a bit of both. He wants a big tent for the Democrats. And for these midterms, as Gen Z voters are starting to sour on Trump, he’s getting one.

His first order of business: reframing the party’s messaging. In 2024, he said, young people fell for a “Trump vision of the country that the Democrats didn’t have, these big, bold ideas: Drill, baby, drill. Build the wall.” Kamala Harris’ messaging, on the other hand, was harder to follow. “Her policy was: ‘If you are a homebuyer under the age of 25 and you live in a certain area, you may be qualified for a $23,000 tax deduction, but only if you live in x, y, and z states,’ ” Mockler said. “It’s like: Wait a minute, you’re starting to lose me on the nitty-gritty of this.”

On a recent episode of What Next, host Mary Harris spoke to Mockler about the role of nuance in viral debate videos and what it would take for Democrats to win the zoomers. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Mary Harris: I think of you as a photo negative of Charlie Kirk. You’re both from the Midwest, you both dropped out of college, and you both have built these political media empires. In the 2024 election, Gen Z—especially Gen Z men—had a real impact. As you’re out there talking with people in your generation, are you seeing younger voters sour on Donald Trump? 

Adam Mockler: Younger voters absolutely are souring on Trump. Now, I need to provide some context as to how younger voters view the 2024 election. A lot of young people weren’t paying attention to the first Trump administration. I was in middle school and near the beginning of high school when he was first president. Most young people were not super locked in during those years to what was happening in the White House.

So Trump was like a vibe. It wasn’t like a real thing. 

It was like a vibe. Most young people’s vibe of that time was, “Hey, summer 2017, summer 2018 was a good time. I don’t remember things being expensive because my parents were paying for things. That seemed like a good time, right?” So when Trump began to run in 2023 and ’24, he was able to capitalize on the fact that many young people didn’t see what he was like as an executive. He was able to say: “No new wars, I’m going to fix the economy on Day 1, I’m going to do this, this, and this.” He came with these bold ideas and somehow was able to paint himself as a change agent coming from the outside. That’s not true. He had four years in the White House. He’s a billionaire. He’s not an outsider. But young people, unfortunately, seem to have fallen for that bit.

So when it comes to the economy and war, we’re seeing in real time that he’s doing the opposite. He’s not just somebody who’s starting new wars. He’s actively posting memes about him and Benjamin Netanyahu sitting on the Gaza Strip after it’s been turned into the Trump Strip. All of my generation’s lowest expectations were then beaten by Trump as he goes lower and lower and lower, as he starts these new wars, as gas prices are spiking and the tariffs are on. I think this really bothers a lot of young people. And young people really do care about the topic of Israel and Palestine, and Trump has not delivered in any sense on that. He’s been the opposite of what we expected.

So you’re saying that young voters memory-holed Trump 1. I believe you on that, but that seems like an epic fail on the Democrats’ part. There was plenty of material from Trump 1 that you could have reupped and said, “Hey, guys, maybe don’t vote for this person.” 

It’s a problem with the broader American electorate. I was going to a bunch of Trump rallies before the 2024 election, and you know what topics I would ask about? Jan. 6, stolen elections, and stuff that I cared about. I thought democracy was the issue. I thought Americans cared about Trump trying to overturn an election. And I was humbled so hard on Election Day 2024. I was like: Did I really just spend four months asking Trump supporters about Jan. 6, when that’s something that no American seems to care about? So even though Trump’s first term was memory-holed by young people, the vast majority of people who voted for Trump, the 75 million, also memory-holed it. I do think it was a failure on the Democrats’ side to have a captivating vision and message for the country. During the four years that Joe Biden was president, he lost our message on immigration, so Trump was able to swoop in with the most radical immigration messaging possible. There was no tension on the other side to push back. Biden didn’t have that.

So we’re now a couple of years into the Trump administration, heading into the midterms. There’s definitely evidence that Gen Z is seeing what’s happening, as you’re saying, and being like, Huh, this isn’t what I expected. Is the messaging better now? I don’t know that there’s great evidence that Gen Z is turning toward Democrats.

Well, we have a few good examples: people like Zohran Mamdani, Abdul El-Sayed, AOC, who are really captivating. We also have even more moderate Democrats, like Abigail Spanberger, who’s passing good legislation. I think this does increase and improve our messaging. Trump is also leaving all these openings. Young people see that this administration is starting wars; we’re almost 200 days into the Iran war, which they said was going to be 28 days long. The Democratic Party needs to reclaim the mantle of being the anti-war party. We still need to fix a lot, but some candidates are really starting to understand how to message. They’re going on more podcasts. Pete Buttigieg is going on Andrew Schulz and these other comedians’ shows. Theo Von is having on more Democrats. We’re starting to get there.

You’ve said in the past that liberals are losing the clip war, essentially. I see your work as trying to push back on that, to create enough content that can flood people’s feeds and combat what they would naturally see there, which might be more conservative messaging. Is that how you view your project?

That’s a big part of it. Donald Trump has turned basically every single governmental agency into a meme account on Twitter right now. I swear to God, the Department of Interior is, for some reason, posting memes of immigrants being hauled off. The “Department of War” is posting edits of wars happening in the Middle East. The White House account is shitposts right now about deporting immigrants and starting wars.

We need our own volume. If I open Twitter right now and go to Elon Musk’s feed, I guarantee he’s tweeted hundreds of times over the past week about trans people or immigrants. He’s always pushing these far-right messages. On the left, we need that same amount of volume, but we need to stick up for affirmative liberal values. It’s easy to flood the internet with fake videos of stolen elections. That’s what Trump did: A.I. videos of people planting ballot boxes in Wisconsin and Michigan. It’s much harder to flood the internet with real, factual videos about how elections deserve to be safe and secure and you shouldn’t deny elections. The facts are messy or nuanced. Reality is rather boring at times, so there needs to be some sort of explosive, in-your-face version of liberalism that tries to fight for human dignity and social harmony and all these things that we care about, while also being a little bit aggressive.

The way you do that is primarily through debate, right? You’re taking other people’s work or information and you’re finding a way to manipulate it, make it more metabolizable for the American public. Debate is one way to do that, but I’ve got to say, I struggle with that format. I worry that dunking on people doesn’t necessarily change their minds. Have you had an internal debate about that? 

The goal is actually never to just dunk on people. There’s a few clips out there of me, when I first started going to Trump rallies, genuinely changing someone’s mind. Dunking on people doesn’t change their mind—you’re right. Having genuine conversation can change people’s minds, but you also have to remember the battlefield we’re on right now. It’s not just about changing the mind of the person you’re talking to. It’s that after you clip this up, it will have millions and millions of views across the internet.

I did something with Jubilee Media a few months back, where I did a Surrounded episode, and some people were asking me, “Do you really want to go on this platform and try to dunk on people?” In my mindset, if I cede this platform to the other side, then who’s going to get to do Jubilee? Ben Shapiro? Would I rather 30 Ben Shapiro clips out there of him dunking on college students that are liberal and don’t really know what they’re talking about, or would I rather have some narrative control about election fraud, gay rights, social harmony, human dignity, and ICE? And 10 out of 10 times, I would rather have my clips and my views being pushed. So the goal isn’t always to maximally dunk on somebody.

You’re doing your own debate show now, but when you describe it more fully, you talk about conversation; you talk about creating dialog at a time when America is uniquely divided. And then the headline for it on YouTube is “I Changed a MAGA Voter’s Mind in 20 Minutes.” It’s not quite dunking, but it’s like you have to play to the algorithm. I think that constrains what you’re able to do.

I agree. It’s something my team and I talk about all the time: the trade-off of playing to the algorithm versus staying true to what you’d want to do. This trade-off almost always falls on the side of maximizing your reach and volume. news.text: Democrats have successfully flipped at least 12 seats in their favor since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House, and they are hoping to flip a few more as the November midterms approach. news.title: What Luigi Mangione’s celebrity says about Gen Z
news.text:
After Luigi Mangione was arrested in December 2024 in connection with the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, the internet did what it often does: It turned something serious into a joke.

Nearly two years later, on Aug. 14, 2026, Mangione pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges and admitted to shooting Thompson. He’s now contesting second-degree murder and related charges in New York state, where his trial is on hold while his attorneys argue much of the case should be dismissed, saying his federal guilty plea means New York would be punishing him twice for the same conduct.

After Mangione’s plea, U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said “there can be no celebrity in assassination.”

Nonetheless, Mangione has become a celebrity.

Viral memes, in 2024 and now, have romanticized him as a popular – and incredibly attractive – man of the people who made corporate elites within the American health insurance industry afraid.

Some of these memes adhered to conventional forms of political satire. One, for example, quoted a speech from the movie “A Bug’s Life,” in which a villainous grasshopper argues for the need to punish the movie’s ant protagonist to keep the other ants in line. In this meme, the political point was clear: Elites preserve power by making examples of insignificant ants who dare to challenge them.

The point was less clear with other memes, including celebrations of Mangione’s fashion-forward shackled ankles in court and mock Burger King advertisements referencing the fact that a McDonald’s employee had been the one to call law enforcement on him: “Burger King: We won’t turn you in to the Feds.” Rather than being ironic, they are unserious.

Nonetheless, memes like those received serious reactions from social commentators and political pundits who interpreted them as evidence that America’s young adults are nihilistic and morally indifferent.

As an experimental psychologist who studies moral judgments about real-world controversies, I have examined these attitudes toward Mangione and the humor surrounding him online.

I believe these reactions are better understood not as a rejection of values but as a refusal to participate in conversations that feel selective and disconnected from young people’s broader economic and political frustrations. In my assessment, Gen Z’s dark and nonsensical humor does not show a lack of moral values, but it’s instead the product of its desire to engage in more authentic conversations about what they believe.

Alienation, not indifference

Research shows deep levels of alienation among Gen Z, or young people born between 1997 and 2012. Having grown up with smartphones and social media, this generation has come of age in an increasingly online world. Despite the internet’s capacity for instantaneous interaction, followers have proved a poor replacement for friends.

Gen Z is among the most socially isolated and psychologically distressed generations on record. Compared with prior generations, fewer friendships and romantic relationships have left many young adults craving connection and solidarity. This alienation is also evident in their skepticism toward institutions and traditional narratives about values.

Many are pessimistic about achieving the American Dream and question the value of higher education. What was once considered the optimal vehicle for living a better life is instead viewed as a barrier.

If the American Dream feels out of reach, and college seems like an expensive obstacle, calls to take them seriously may feel inauthentic, alienating and absurd.

When seriousness gets suspended

Discussions about values require some seriousness if they are to resonate with their audience.

If, for example, a commencement speaker praising the value of artificial intelligence is met with jeers from graduates – as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt was in May 2026 – the speaker’s message is immediately rendered inert.

These students’ jeers fell short of offering an argument against the speaker’s claims; instead, they created an atmosphere that prevented those claims from receiving consideration. For graduates pessimistic about AI’s implications for the labor market, claims professing its value feel inauthentic.

Together, their jeers not only provided an escape from what felt like an alienating and inauthentic message about the value of AI, but they also created a sense of solidarity through a shared suspension of seriousness.

Humor offers an escape

Far from being unique to Mangione, this suspension of seriousness recurs throughout online meme culture.

The OceanGate implosion prompted similar memes, including one depicting a pod of orcas with the caption “The water is safe, send more billionaires.”

Even Charlie Kirk’s assassination became material. In a trend known as “Kirkification,” users superimposed his face onto images ranging from the Mona Lisa to women in bikinis, transforming a grim event into a shared absurdity.

In my assessment, Gen Z’s creation and circulation of memes offers an escape from otherwise serious conversations – for example, conversations about the value of the UnitedHealthcare CEO’s life. This may be especially true when demands to condemn Mangione appear to ignore inequities within an American health insurance system perceived as corrupt and unjust.

Although commentators often dismiss Gen Z’s humor as nonsensical or nihilistic meme slop, scholarship suggests that it acts as a collaborative coping mechanism, driven by a desire for authenticity.

Memes about Mangione, or even campus lookalike contests centered on him, fall short of offering a precise moral argument in favor of largely suspending seriousness.

This style of humor can be seen in Mangione’s decision to leave a backpack containing Monopoly money in Central Park. It was seen, too, on shell casings recovered after Kirk’s killing, which included video game commands, a sexually suggestive internet saying and “if you read this you are gay lmao.”

Miscast explanations of nihilism

With the help of approximately a dozen undergraduate students, I examined the psychological and situational factors associated with Gen Z’s reactions to Mangione and other events – like Kirk’s assassination and the Kamala Harris is “Brat” phenomenon during the 2024 presidential election – in two studies currently under review.

Our findings indicate that favorable attitudes toward Mangione were associated not only with superficial factors, such as his perceived attractiveness, but also with higher levels of political cynicism.

Perceived systemic bias in the American justice system, for example, was addressed in a meme depicting Mangione walking into court with the text “You can kill dozens of kids and get a lesser sentence because their lives don’t matter as much as a CEO’s.” Federal prosecutors were seeking the death penalty against Mangione for a charge a judge dismissed in January 2026.

Casting Gen Z’s reactions as nihilistic obscures the values and institutional distrust connected to them and fails to appreciate their egalitarian and pragmatic ideals. Dismissing them may deepen the alienation that allowed the death of a father of two to become a joke.

Why simple moral messages alienate

Although political commentators disagree about how to interpret the response to Mangione, many accept a seemingly basic principle: Killing should never be justified.

Yet decades of research on moral judgment shows that people do not apply that principle consistently. Instead, in certain situations, like in the famous “trolley problem,” people frequently judge killing to be morally permissible – especially when that killing is expected to promote the well-being of others.

Simplistic and sweeping moral injunctions not only fail to appreciate people’s actual moral attitudes, but they also eliminate the possibility of having authentic and nuanced conversations.

Those conversations need not end by endorsing Mangione as a sympathetic figure. However, an open and authentic conversation about Mangione cannot be realized in spaces that require all discussion of the event to be reduced to affirmations that, as has been advocated by some, “Murder is bad. Period.”

Such requirements can make conversations about significant moral issues – even controversial ones, like the morality of Mangione’s actions – little more than demands for conformity. In this case, those boundaries risk ignoring and, thus, further alienating Gen Z.

Reactions to recent coverage illustrate this concern. A popular Reddit post published just after the guilty plea complained that “media corporations are not reporting his entire statement,” pointing to Mangione’s account in court of UnitedHealthcare answering his email within an hour when he posed as a prospective investor – a contrast, he said, with his previous dealings with insurers. In my assessment, these reactions are revealing: Users were not necessarily upset that Mangione was portrayed negatively but that information they considered relevant to understanding his motivation was excluded from the conversation.

Time will tell whether Mangione is remembered, as his critics expect, as little more than a morally bankrupt flash in the pan or, by those sympathetic to him, as a martyr who reinvigorated a long-standing debate about healthcare in the U.S.

I believe that outcome will depend not only on Gen Z’s values, but also on how young people experience the conversational spaces in which Mangione’s crime, motives and punishment are discussed. If those spaces are perceived as selective or inauthentic, continued alienation may leave them laughing when seriousness is most required.

Utah Valley University undergraduate student Sebastian Trias contributed to this research.

Given how new the issues of advanced AI and AI data centers are, the issue hasn’t yet settled into opposing partisan camps. Republican officials are generally more likely to support the AI industry, following President Donald Trump’s lead, but the sentiment isn’t unanimous.

Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-WI), the Republican nominee in the Wisconsin gubernatorial election, has leaned into anti-AI sentiment, debuting an ad on Monday calling his Democratic opponent David Crowley “Data Center David Crowley.”

In the ad, Tiffany leaned into fears about water waste and Big Tech, while claiming under Crowley’s policies Wisconsinites would foot the bill. The Republican made clear his own anti-AI view in the ad’s caption on YouTube.

“Tiffany has been clear that there should be no new data centers in Wisconsin unless they meet strict standards that protect our state: no taxpayer subsidies, no development on productive farmland, no higher utility costs passed on to families and businesses, no secret NDAs, and full local control,” he said.

Even elected allies of Trump have begun distancing themselves from the AI industry. Gov. Greg Abbott (R-TX) ordered an audit of hundreds of AI data center construction projects earlier in the summer, which could delay their construction for several more months.

“I’d make clear already: Any AI data center even thinking about coming here, they got to bring their own money, bring their own power, reuse their own water, and do it in a way that reduces the cost of electricity for residents across our state,” he said. “We must eliminate the tax break they are getting. They must be responsible for funding their own projects here in Texas. We will get that done.”

DEMOCRATS LEAD OPPOSITION TO DATA CENTERS, THOUGH POPULARITY IS LOW ACROSS THE POLITICAL SPECTRUM: POLL

Backlash against AI data centers has increased over the first half of 2026. In January, 37% of respondents supported constructing a data center within 3 miles of their home, while 28% opposed it. This was reversed in July, with 41% of respondents opposing the idea of building a data center within 3 miles of their home, while support collapsed to just 24%.

Support fell across the political spectrum but was particularly pronounced among Democrats. Poll respondents’ opposition to data center construction within 3 miles of their home shot from 33% in January to 53% in July among Americans who voted for Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, compared to a 26% to 33% jump in opposition among Trump voters.

news.title: Redistricting gives Republicans an edge, but affordability will decide the midterms
news.text: Republicans may be winning the redistricting war while losing the voters they need to build a lasting majority. The latest Fox News Power Rankings reveal a serious warning for Republicans. The new maps favor the GOP, but the political environment favors Democrats. The GOP could gain a dozen seats, including up to nine in Florida and Texas, due to redistricting. However, House Democrats expanded their midterm target list to 58 Republican-held districts, adding 12 seats in territory President Donald Trump carried. While expanded targets do not guarantee Democratic victories, they signal that Democrats see an opening among dissatisfied voters. Republicans must confront this challenge before the November midterms, but they must also recognize the opportunity to strengthen the party for future elections. Redistricting can give overlooked voters a stronger voice, attract better candidates and provide Republicans the stability needed to govern, but it cannot generate public confidence or voter enthusiasm. Current polling signals the urgency. Seventy-five percent of voters said inflation had caused financial hardship, while 54% expected the economy to worsen. Democrats lead the generic congressional ballot 53% to 46%, with voters preferring them on inflation by 10 points and the economy by nine. Democrats also hold an enthusiasm advantage, with 68% saying they are extremely motivated to vote in November compared with 57% of Republicans. In counties likely to determine control of Congress, where Trump and Kamala Harris finished within 10 points in 2024, Democrats lead the congressional ballot 59% to 41%. A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll found voters preferring Democrats over Republicans on the economy for the first time in nearly a decade. While the advantage is only one point, it is significant because Republicans risk losing their historic advantage on the issue that often determines elections. IT’S NOT THE ECONOMY, STUPID. AMERICANS VOTE BASED ON THEIR PERSONAL ECONOMY There is no doubt that Republicans should use every lawful political advantage available to them. Democrats certainly will. Republicans deserve credit for pursuing redistricting that was both strategic and necessary to secure fairer representation for voters who had previously been trapped in gerrymandered districts. Republicans now have an enormous opportunity to make the case for the promises they have already kept, including securing the border and delivering historic tax relief through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The next step is to explain what additional measures Republicans will take to confront the affordability crisis. Republicans cannot redistrict their way out of an affordability crisis because congressional maps will not lower grocery bills, make housing affordable or reduce the cost of gasoline, childcare and healthcare. Map victories will not convince the younger generation that hard work will lead to homeownership or reassure a small-business owner whose revenue is being overtaken by higher labor, energy and borrowing costs. Voters judge the economy through weekly bills, not maps. Even voters who agree with Republicans on immigration, crime and cultural issues may conclude that the party in power has not delivered. The path is clear: continue lowering energy costs, restrain federal spending, remove barriers to home construction, protect small businesses and provide additional tax relief for working families. Every Republican measure should answer a simple question: Does this make life more affordable for Americans? Republicans won the presidency by promising safety, security and the restoration of the American Dream. Voters will measure delivery at the grocery store, the gas pump and the kitchen table. A majority gives Republicans enough votes to elect a speaker, but public trust gives them the support needed to lead the country. Redistricting buys Republicans time to protect the majority, but that time is valuable only if used to govern. If Republicans deliver affordability, security and economic opportunity, they can build a lasting coalition. If they mistake favorable district lines for voter approval, today’s safe districts could become the epicenter of tomorrow’s political earthquake.
